strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: forecasting pre-training loss to support hyperparameter selection directly on the target model. The connection to data-mixture selection gives the work a concrete practical motivation.

The position-wise hyperbolic description is interpretable and supported across two model sizes and both ID and OOD validation data. The reported fits and the direct loss-change plots provide useful empirical evidence about training dynamics.

Evaluation includes future-loss prediction from partial training trajectories and completed training runs for the selection application. The selected mixtures improve perplexity in all four reported settings and benchmark performance in 12 of 14 model–task comparisons.
The appendix provides useful architecture, training, software-version, and weighting-strategy details.
weaknesses: The central baseline comparison has an unresolved soundness problem. Table 1 reports strongly negative R² for power-law fits evaluated on the complete fitting data. The stated function, L=(p1*x)^p2+p3, can represent the mean predictor through its exponent and offset, so an unconstrained least-squares optimum should achieve R²≥0. The reported values require an explanation of optimization failures or undisclosed constraints. Corrected fits and forecasting comparisons are necessary before accepting the claimed superiority.

The experiments do not isolate the benefit of modeling token positions. The proposed predictor incorporates the known cosine learning-rate schedule, while the aggregate-loss baselines lack this information. A direct aggregate-loss baseline using the same piecewise logarithmic/cosine structure is needed. Moreover, the main forecasting evidence covers only 468M and 1.2B models, 1024-token contexts, and one 400B-token cosine training regime; broader temporal-scaling claims exceed this evidence.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence is promising but incomplete. Selection extrapolates from 10B to 400B tokens, whereas the dedicated forecasting experiments begin at 40B tokens. Candidate-wise predicted and final losses, ranking accuracy, and uncertainty are not reported. Averaging the last five checkpoints does not establish robustness across independent runs, particularly for the modest perplexity improvements.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified: nonlinear-fitting initialization and constraints, the residual-based outlier rejection rule, the number and exact weights of mixture candidates, and random seeds. No implementation or training-trajectory release is identified. These omissions affect reproduction of the central fitting and selection procedures.

The numerical results need reconciliation. Substituting Figure 1’s parameters into Eqs. (10) and (2), with sequence length 1024, gives ID perplexities of approximately 6.97 and 6.17. Table 4 reports default-practice values of 8.62 and 7.52 under the referenced training setup. Any differences in runs or evaluation aggregation should be explained.

The conclusion about position weighting is stronger than its support. Equal late-stage loss-decrease rates follow partly from manually freezing a0 and a1; Figure 6 provides supporting observations, but equal rates do not establish optimal weighting. Three fixed suppression strategies support the competitiveness of uniform weighting only within those comparisons. Overall, the baseline and reproducibility concerns require substantive revision before a positive Findings recommendation.
